prompt: Determine the number of real solutions to the equation $\sqrt{2-x^2}=\sqrt[3]{3-x^3}$.

solutions.title: Sixth powers and a sum of squares
solutions.body:
A solution needs $|x|\le\sqrt2$. Raising both (nonnegative) sides to the sixth power, a solution satisfies $(2-x^2)^3=(3-x^3)^2$, i.e.
$$f(x):=2x^6-6x^4-6x^3+12x^2+1=0 .$$
We show $f(x)>0$ for $x\le\sqrt2$. Let
$$g(x)=2x^6-6x^4-4\sqrt2x^3+12x^2=2x^2(x-\sqrt2)^2(x^2+2\sqrt2x+3)$$
(expand: $(x-\sqrt2)^2(x^2+2\sqrt2x+3)=x^4-3x^2-2\sqrt2x+6$). Since $x^2+2\sqrt2x+3=(x+\sqrt2)^2+1>0$, $g(x)\ge0$ for all $x$. Now
$$f(x)-g(x)=(4\sqrt2-6)x^3+1,$$
which is decreasing in $x$ because $4\sqrt2-6<0$. So for $x\le\sqrt2$,
$$f(x)-g(x)\ge(4\sqrt2-6)\cdot2\sqrt2+1=17-12\sqrt2>0,$$
because $17^2=289>288=(12\sqrt2)^2$. Hence $f(x)>g(x)\ge0$ on $(-\infty,\sqrt2]$, and the equation has no real solution.

**Answer: $0$.**

solutions.title: Compare the common value with $x$
solutions.body:
Suppose $x$ is a solution and let $t\ge0$ be the common value. Then
$$t^2+x^2=2,\qquad t^3+x^3=3 .$$
From the first equation $t\le\sqrt2$ and $|x|\le\sqrt2$.

* If $x\le0$: $t^3=3-x^3\ge3$, but $t^3\le2\sqrt2<3$. Impossible.
* If $x>0$: both $t,x$ lie in $[0,\sqrt2]$, so
$$t^3+x^3=t\cdot t^2+x\cdot x^2\le\sqrt2\,(t^2+x^2)=2\sqrt2<3 .$$
Impossible.

So there are **no** real solutions.

prompt: Evaluate $$\int_0^a\frac{dx}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\qquad\text{for } -\pi/2<a<\pi.$$ Use your answer to show that $$\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\cos x+\sin x}=\ln2.$$

solutions.title: Half-angle substitution
solutions.body:
On $(-\pi/2,\pi)$ the denominator $1+\cos x+\sin x=1+\sqrt2\sin(x+\frac\pi4)$ is positive (because $x+\frac\pi4\in(-\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}4)$, where $\sin>-\frac1{\sqrt2}$), so the integral exists.

Let $t=\tan(x/2)$; as $x$ runs over $(-\pi/2,\pi)$, $x/2\in(-\pi/4,\pi/2)$ and $t$ increases over $(-1,\infty)$. We have
$$\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\qquad \sin x=2\sin\tfrac x2\cos\tfrac x2=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\qquad dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}.$$
Hence $1+\cos x+\sin x=\dfrac{2(1+t)}{1+t^2}$ and
$$\int_0^a\frac{dx}{1+\cos x+\sin x}=\int_0^{\tan(a/2)}\frac{dt}{1+t}=\ln\!\Big(1+\tan\frac a2\Big),$$
which is well defined because $1+\tan(a/2)>0$.

For $a=\pi/2$: $\tan(\pi/4)=1$, so the integral is $\ln2$.

(Equivalently, $\ln(1+\tan\frac a2)=\frac12\ln\frac{1+\sin a}{1+\cos a}+\frac12\ln2$.)

**Answer: $\ln\big(1+\tan\frac a2\big)$.** ∎

solutions.title: Factor the denominator directly
solutions.body:
Using $1+\cos x=2\cos^2\frac x2$ and $\sin x=2\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2$,
$$1+\cos x+\sin x=2\cos^2\tfrac x2\Big(1+\tan\tfrac x2\Big).$$
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan\dfrac x2=\dfrac{1}{2\cos^2(x/2)}$,
$$\frac{1}{1+\cos x+\sin x}=\frac{\frac{d}{dx}\big(1+\tan\frac x2\big)}{1+\tan\frac x2}=\frac{d}{dx}\ln\Big(1+\tan\frac x2\Big)$$
on $(-\pi/2,\pi)$, where $1+\tan\frac x2>0$. Integrating from $0$ to $a$ gives $\ln(1+\tan\frac a2)$, and $a=\frac\pi2$ gives $\ln2$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $P$ be a point in its interior. Suppose $\angle BAP=10^\circ$, $\angle ABP=20^\circ$, $\angle PCA=30^\circ$ and $\angle PAC=40^\circ$. Find $\angle PBC$.

solutions.title: Law of sines
solutions.body:
Let $\theta=\angle PBC$. The angles of the small triangles are:
* $\triangle APB$: $\angle APB=180^\circ-10^\circ-20^\circ=150^\circ$;
* $\triangle APC$: $\angle APC=180^\circ-40^\circ-30^\circ=110^\circ$;
* hence $\angle BPC=360^\circ-150^\circ-110^\circ=100^\circ$ and $\angle PCB=80^\circ-\theta$, with $0<\theta<80^\circ$.

Scale so that $AB=1$. The law of sines in $\triangle APB$ gives $AP=\dfrac{\sin20^\circ}{\sin150^\circ}=2\sin20^\circ$ and $BP=2\sin10^\circ$. In $\triangle APC$,
$$CP=AP\,\frac{\sin40^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=4\sin20^\circ\sin40^\circ=2(\cos20^\circ-\cos60^\circ)=2\cos20^\circ-1 .$$
In $\triangle BPC$, $\dfrac{CP}{\sin\theta}=\dfrac{BP}{\sin(80^\circ-\theta)}$, and $\sin(80^\circ-\theta)=\cos(\theta+10^\circ)$, so
$$(2\cos20^\circ-1)\cos(\theta+10^\circ)=2\sin10^\circ\sin\theta .$$
Product-to-sum: $2\cos20^\circ\cos(\theta+10^\circ)=\cos(\theta+30^\circ)+\cos(\theta-10^\circ)$ and $2\sin10^\circ\sin\theta=\cos(\theta-10^\circ)-\cos(\theta+10^\circ)$. Substituting,
$$\cos(\theta+30^\circ)+\cos(\theta-10^\circ)-\cos(\theta+10^\circ)=\cos(\theta-10^\circ)-\cos(\theta+10^\circ),$$
so $\cos(\theta+30^\circ)=0$. With $30^\circ<\theta+30^\circ<110^\circ$ this gives $\theta+30^\circ=90^\circ$.

**Answer: $\angle PBC=60^\circ$.**

solutions.title: Trigonometric Ceva
solutions.body:
With $\theta=\angle PBC$ and $\angle PCB=80^\circ-\theta$ as above, the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem for the concurrent cevians $AP,BP,CP$ reads
$$\frac{\sin\angle BAP}{\sin\angle PAC}\cdot\frac{\sin\angle ACP}{\sin\angle PCB}\cdot\frac{\sin\angle CBP}{\sin\angle PBA}=1,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{\sin\theta}{\sin(80^\circ-\theta)}=\frac{\sin40^\circ\sin20^\circ}{\sin10^\circ\sin30^\circ}.$$
The left side is strictly increasing on $(0^\circ,80^\circ)$, so there is at most one solution. Check $\theta=60^\circ$: we need $\sin10^\circ\sin60^\circ=2\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ$. Now
$$2\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ=\sin40^\circ(1-\cos40^\circ)=\sin40^\circ-\tfrac12\sin80^\circ,\qquad \sin10^\circ\sin60^\circ=\tfrac12(\cos50^\circ-\cos70^\circ)=\tfrac12(\sin40^\circ-\sin20^\circ),$$
and these agree because $\sin40^\circ+\sin20^\circ=2\sin30^\circ\cos10^\circ=\sin80^\circ$. Hence $\angle PBC=60^\circ$.

prompt: Let $P$ be an interior point of a triangle of area $T$. Through the point $P$, draw lines parallel to the three sides, partitioning the triangle into three triangles and three parallelograms. Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the areas of the three triangles. Prove that $\sqrt T=\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c$.
answer: The three small triangles are similar to the big one, and their sides parallel to one side of the triangle add up (via the parallelograms) to that whole side, so $\sqrt{a/T}+\sqrt{b/T}+\sqrt{c/T}=1$.

solutions.title: Similar triangles along one side
solutions.body:
Let the triangle be $ABC$. Let the line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ meet $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$; the line through $P$ parallel to $CA$ meet $AB$ at $F$ and $BC$ at $G$; the line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ meet $BC$ at $H$ and $CA$ at $K$.

The three small triangles are $FDP$ (on $AB$), $GHP$ (on $BC$) and $KEP$ (on $CA$). Each has its three sides parallel to the three sides of $ABC$, so each is similar to $ABC$, with ratio $\sqrt{\text{area}/T}$; say the areas of $FDP,GHP,KEP$ are $a,b,c$ (any labelling works by symmetry). Their sides parallel to $AB$ are $FD$, $HP$ and $PK$, of lengths $\sqrt{a/T}\,AB$, $\sqrt{b/T}\,AB$, $\sqrt{c/T}\,AB$.

The quadrilateral $AFPK$ has $AF\parallel KP$ (both along/parallel to $AB$) and $FP\parallel AK$ (both parallel to $CA$), so it is a parallelogram and $AF=KP$. Similarly $BDPH$ is a parallelogram ($BD\parallel PH$, $DP\parallel BH$), so $DB=PH$. On segment $AB$ the points lie in the order $A,F,D,B$ (see the second solution), hence
$$AB=AF+FD+DB=KP+FD+PH=\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac cT}+\sqrt{\tfrac aT}+\sqrt{\tfrac bT}\Big)AB .$$
Dividing by $AB$ and multiplying by $\sqrt T$: $\sqrt T=\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c$. ∎

solutions.title: Barycentric coordinates
solutions.body:
Write $P=\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C$ with $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$ (barycentric coordinates; positive since $P$ is interior).

Moving parallel to $BC$ keeps the coefficient of $A$ fixed, moving parallel to $CA$ keeps the coefficient of $B$ fixed. On $AB$ the coefficient of $C$ is $0$. Hence the two lines through $P$ meet $AB$ at
$$F=(1-\beta)A+\beta B\ \ (\text{line}\parallel CA),\qquad D=\alpha A+(1-\alpha)B\ \ (\text{line}\parallel BC).$$
Measured from $A$, these points are at distances $\beta\,AB$ and $(1-\alpha)AB$, and $\beta<1-\alpha$ since $\gamma>0$. So $FD=(1-\alpha-\beta)AB=\gamma\,AB$. The triangle $FDP$ is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $\gamma$, so its area is $\gamma^2T$.

By the same computation on the other sides, the other two small triangles have areas $\alpha^2T$ and $\beta^2T$. Therefore
$$\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\sqrt T=\sqrt T .\ ∎$$

prompt:
Let $f(x,y)=\dfrac{x+y}{2}$, $g(x,y)=\sqrt{xy}$, $h(x,y)=\dfrac{2xy}{x+y}$, and let
$$S=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\mid a\ne b\text{ and } f(a,b),\,g(a,b),\,h(a,b)\in\mathbb N\},$$
where $\mathbb N$ denotes the positive integers. Find the minimum of $f$ over $S$.

solutions.title: Parametrise all pairs in $S$
solutions.body:
Let $(a,b)\in S$, $d=\gcd(a,b)$, $a=dm$, $b=dn$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$, $m\ne n$.

* $g(a,b)=d\sqrt{mn}\in\mathbb N$ means $mn$ is a perfect square; as $\gcd(m,n)=1$, both are squares: $m=s^2$, $n=t^2$, $\gcd(s,t)=1$, $s\ne t$.
* $h(a,b)=\dfrac{2d^2s^2t^2}{d(s^2+t^2)}=\dfrac{2ds^2t^2}{s^2+t^2}\in\mathbb N$. Since $\gcd(s^2+t^2,s^2t^2)=1$ (a prime dividing $s^2+t^2$ and $s$ would divide $t$), we need $s^2+t^2\mid 2d$: $2d=k(s^2+t^2)$ for some $k\in\mathbb N$.
* Then $f(a,b)=\dfrac{d(s^2+t^2)}{2}=\dfrac{k(s^2+t^2)^2}{4}$.

Now $s\ne t$ are coprime positive integers.

* If $s^2+t^2$ is odd, $f\in\mathbb N$ forces $4\mid k$; also $s^2+t^2\ge1+4=5$. So $f\ge\frac{4\cdot25}{4}=25$.
* If $s^2+t^2$ is even, $s,t$ are both odd (not both even, as they are coprime) and distinct, so $s^2+t^2\ge1+9=10$ and $f\ge\frac{100}{4}=25$.

So $f\ge25$ on $S$. Equality occurs: $s=1,t=2,k=4$ gives $d=10$, $(a,b)=(10,40)$ with $f=25$, $g=20$, $h=16$; and $s=1,t=3,k=1$ gives $d=5$, $(a,b)=(5,45)$ with $f=25$, $g=15$, $h=9$.

**Answer: $25$.**

solutions.title: Use the relation $g^2=fh$
solutions.body:
For any $a,b>0$, $f\cdot h= rac{a+b}2\cdot rac{2ab}{a+b}=ab=g^2$, and $h<g<f$ when $a
e b$. Also $a,b$ are the roots of $z^2-2fz+g^2=0$, so $a,b=f\pm\sqrt{f^2-g^2}$; thus $f^2-g^2$ must be a perfect square, say $e^2$, with $e>0$.

So we need positive integers $f>g>h$ with $g^2=fh$ and $f^2=g^2+e^2$. Then $(e,g,f)$ is a Pythagorean triple and $f\mid g^2$. Search $f$ upward among hypotenuses of Pythagorean triples: $5$ ($g\in\{3,4\}$: $5
mid9,16$), $10$ ($g\in\{6,8\}$: $10
mid36,64$), $13$ ($g\in\{5,12\}$), $15$ ($g\in\{9,12\}$: $15
mid81,144$), $17$ ($g\in\{8,15\}$), $20$ ($g\in\{12,16\}$: $20
mid144,256$) — all fail ($13,17$ are primes not dividing $g$). For $f=25$, $g=15$: $25\mid225$, $h=9$, $e=20$, giving $(a,b)=(5,45)$. (Hypotenuses below $25$ are exactly $5,10,13,15,17,20$.) Hence the minimum is $25$.

prompt: Let $f(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $f(1)=-1$, $f(4)=2$ and $f(8)=34$. Suppose $n\in\mathbb Z$ is an integer such that $f(n)=n^2-4n-18$. Determine all possible values for $n$.

solutions.title: Factor out the three known roots
solutions.body:
Let $g(x)=f(x)-x^2+4x-2$. Then $g(1)=-1-1+4-2=0$, $g(4)=2-16+16-2=0$, $g(8)=34-64+32-2=0$. Since $g\in\mathbb Z[x]$ and we divide by monic factors,
$$g(x)=(x-1)(x-4)(x-8)\,q(x),\qquad q\in\mathbb Z[x].$$
If $f(n)=n^2-4n-18$ then $g(n)=-18-2=-20$, so
$$(n-1)(n-4)(n-8)\,q(n)=-20 .$$
Thus $n-1$, $n-4$, $n-8$ are divisors of $20$ whose product divides $20$. The divisors of $20$ are $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm5,\pm10,\pm20$. The numbers $d=n-1$ and $d-7=n-8$ must both be divisors; going through the list, $d-7$ equals $-6,-5,-3,-2,3,13$ for $d=1,2,4,5,10,20$ and $-8,-9,-11,-12,-17,-27$ for $d=-1,\dots,-20$, so only $d=2$ and $d=5$ work, i.e. $n\in\{3,6\}$. Then
$$n=3:\ 2\cdot(-1)\cdot(-5)=10,\qquad n=6:\ 5\cdot2\cdot(-2)=-20,$$
both dividing $20$, with $q(n)=-2$ and $q(n)=1$ respectively.

Both values really occur: with $q(x)=-2$, $f(x)=-2(x-1)(x-4)(x-8)+x^2-4x+2$ satisfies the three conditions and $f(3)=-20+(9-12+2)=-21=3^2-4\cdot3-18$; with $q(x)=1$, $f(x)=(x-1)(x-4)(x-8)+x^2-4x+2$ gives $f(6)=-20+14=-6=36-24-18$.

**Answer: $n=3$ or $n=6$.**
